title: Orcas Are Smashing Sunfish Like Piñatas
summary:
Imagine a piñata at a birthday party. Now imagine an orca. Scientists have filmed orcas doing something wild: slamming into sunfish hard enough to make them explode.

In 2024 and 2025, researchers watched this in the Gulf of California. One adult orca held a dead sharp-tail sunfish steady. A second orca rammed into it — smashing the fish to bits.

"I was absolutely gobsmacked," said Marianne Nyegaard, a marine biologist in New Zealand who wasn't part of the study. "I thought it was the coolest thing I had ever seen."

Why do they do it? Maybe to break the huge fish into smaller bites for young orcas. After one explosion, a young orca ate the small pieces. Sharp-tail sunfish can grow up to 10 feet long — that's taller than a basketball hoop!

Or maybe it's just fun. Orcas are super social and clever. They work as a team to hunt blue whales, knock penguins off ice, and more.

"Killer whales are highly social animals," said marine biologist Francesca Pancaldi. One activity can give them food, help them bond, and teach young orcas how to hunt.

The study came out July 23 in Frontiers in Ethology.
why_it_matters: It shows animals can have team activities that feed them, teach their young, and hold their family together — a lot like how families and sports teams learn and help each other.

background_read: Orcas, also called killer whales, live in every ocean on Earth and hunt together in family groups called pods.
The Gulf of California is a narrow sea between Mexico's mainland and the long Baja California peninsula, and it is famous for whales, dolphins, and many kinds of fish.
Killer whales are actually a kind of dolphin, not a whale, and they are known for clever teamwork — like knocking penguins off ice or hunting much bigger animals together.
Article_Structure: WHO: Orcas in the Gulf of California, filmed by researchers; marine biologists Marianne Nyegaard and Francesca Pancaldi gave their reactions.
WHAT: Orcas rammed a dead sharp-tail sunfish and smashed it apart, in videos recorded in 2024 and 2025.
WHERE: The Gulf of California, with the study published in the journal Frontiers in Ethology.
WHY: Scientists think the smashing may break the fish into bites for young orcas, or may simply be fun and bonding for these very social animals.

perspectives.description: They filmed the smashing twice and think it is a real, repeated behaviour worth studying, possibly a way to feed young orcas or to share a social moment.
Some experts may say two sightings aren't enough to know whether the orcas do this to eat, to practice hunting, or just for fun.
They see this as more proof that orcas are super smart and social, which is why protecting oceans and orca families matters.
